title: Ancient San Rock Art Debunks Dinosaur and Tusked-Beast Myths, Reveals True Monster Legends
body:
A new study of ancient rock‑paintings in southern Africa suggests that the region’s Indigenous San and Basotho peoples may have recorded encounters with fossilised remains long before modern paleontology, but the creatures they depicted are not the dinosaurs that dominate today’s textbooks. Instead, researchers argue that the enigmatic figures – often described as “monsters” with tusks or massive bodies – are more likely stylised representations of extinct megafauna such as giant mammals, or symbolic composites drawn from oral tradition, challenging a decades‑old hypothesis that prehistoric African art directly mirrors dinosaur anatomy.

The investigation, led by a multidisciplinary team of archaeologists, palaeontologists and ethnographers, re‑examined over two hundred rock‑art sites across the Kalahari and the highlands of Lesotho. Using high‑resolution photogrammetry, pigment analysis and contextual dating techniques, the scholars established a tighter chronological framework for the artworks, placing most of the “monster” motifs between 2,000 and 500 years ago – well after the extinction of non‑avian dinosaurs around 66 million years ago. The timing, they argue, makes it improbable that the artists were observing actual dinosaur fossils in situ; rather, the motifs likely stem from a cultural memory of the region’s Pleistocene megafauna, such as mammoths, giant ground sloths and the now‑extinct African elephant relatives like *Palaeoloxodon*.

The reinterpretation overturns a popular narrative that emerged in the 1970s, when a handful of strikingly detailed San paintings were taken as evidence that Indigenous peoples had identified dinosaur bones and incorporated them into mythic storytelling. That view, while captivating, rested on speculative links between stylised art and skeletal morphology, often ignoring the broader symbolic language of the San and Basotho. The new research highlights that many of the “tusked beasts” bear features – elongated trunks, exaggerated horns and composite limbs – that align more closely with known extinct mammals than with theropod or sauropod dinosaurs. Moreover, oral histories collected from contemporary San communities describe “great beasts” that roamed the land in ancient times, but these narratives focus on size, power and spiritual significance rather than precise anatomical detail.

Contextualising the findings within the wider field of paleo‑art interpretation, the study underscores the pitfalls of projecting modern scientific categories onto prehistoric symbolism. Similar debates have arisen around Australian Aboriginal rock art and North American Native petroglyphs, where alleged dinosaur depictions have been re‑examined and often re‑classified as mythic or allegorical creatures. By applying rigorous dating methods and cross‑disciplinary analysis, the current work adds weight to a growing consensus that ancient peoples were more likely to mythologise the awe‑inspiring remnants of their own megafaunal past than to reconstruct extinct reptiles they never witnessed.

The implications extend beyond academic circles. For Indigenous groups, the reinterpretation offers a more nuanced appreciation of their cultural heritage, recognising that their artistic legacy reflects a sophisticated engagement with the environment and its long‑term changes. It also prompts museums and educational institutions to revisit exhibit narratives that have long presented the San as “early dinosaur hunters,” a trope that can inadvertently marginalise the peoples’ own cosmologies and scientific contributions.

Looking ahead, the research team plans to expand the survey to additional sites in Namibia, Botswana and South Africa, employing portable X‑ray fluorescence (pXRF) and 3‑D laser scanning to capture finer details of pigment composition and technique. By building a larger comparative database of rock‑art motifs and correlating them with regional fossil records, scholars hope to map a more accurate picture of how extinct megafauna shaped Indigenous myth and memory. In doing so, they aim not only to refine our understanding of prehistoric art but also to honour the deep temporal dialogue between humans and the ancient creatures that once shared their world.
